Harlowe turns towards the stairs, his jaw tightening.

“They've discovered something,” he mutters. “And if the Coven comes down here and finds you standing beside an awakened ward, they'll want to know why it answers your blood.”

He looks at you again. His crossbow remains lowered, but his fingers tighten around its stock.

“If you can control that thing, they'll never let you leave this keep. They'll either use you to maintain the binding or bury you beneath it.”

The lock-plate pulses once more. You feel its resonance beneath your skin, like a key turning somewhere deep inside your bones.

Harlowe waits for your decision. You have little time before the Coven arrives, and whatever lies beneath the keep is beginning to stir.

How will you proceed?

choices.text: Reveal the truth: tell Harlowe that the garrison was built over an ancient binding cage and ask for his help.
Use the distraction to activate the lock-plate with your blood, securing the lower vaults before the Coven arrives.
Bar the subterranean iron door, locking Harlowe out while you prepare the lower tunnels for escape.

text.content:
Before another word can be spoken, heavy boots thunder on the stairs above. Voices echo through the stone corridor, followed by the clatter of weapons and the unmistakable rattle of iron lanterns. A garrison patrol is descending.

You turn towards the cellar door. Beyond it lies the armory corridor, the quickest route back towards the main keep. If the guards find you here with a wounded Fae and an unstable lock-anchor, there will be no explaining your way out of it.

Panic tightens your chest.

The heat beneath your collarbone, dormant since the night Highspire burned, suddenly surges through your body. It spreads down your arms and into your fingertips, so intense that you gasp. You reach for the heavy oak door, intending to bar it before the guards arrive.

Your bare palm strikes the iron lock.

The world turns white.

Heat explodes through the mechanism. You wrench your hand away, but the metal has already begun to glow, shifting from dull grey to brilliant orange, then to a white so bright that the shadows vanish from the corridor. Iron runs like liquid beneath your palm. It drips down the lock plate, hissing against the stone, before the entire mechanism fuses into the doorframe.

The smell of burning metal fills your lungs.

You stumble backwards, clutching your hand. There is no wound, no blister, not even a mark upon your skin. Yet the heat continues to pulse beneath it, as though something inside your blood has found a way out.

A deep vibration rolls through the foundations.

The granite walls illuminate with lines of violet light. One rune appears beneath the floor, another across the archway, and then dozens more spread through the stone like veins beneath translucent skin. The markings are ancient, their shapes unfamiliar, yet something about them feels disturbingly intimate.

You recognise the interlocking spiral from your family's seal.

The runes answer the heat in your body. Each pulse travels further into the keep, illuminating hidden channels in the walls and floor. Somewhere above, iron groans against iron. A heavy door slams shut, followed by shouts from the upper corridors.

Outside the cellar, the guards begin rattling the latch.

“Open this door!”

One of them strikes it with the butt of a weapon. The impact sends a shower of sparks from the melted lock.

“What in the bloody hell—?”

“Stand back! Get the quartermaster!”

Their confusion quickly becomes alarm. You hear someone calling for Commander Vane. Another voice orders the corridor cleared. The patrol has realised that whatever happened to the door was no ordinary accident.

Behind you, Balor rises from the darkness.

You had almost forgotten he was there. He moves carefully, one hand pressed against the silver-lit wound in his side. Even injured, he seems unnaturally composed. Violet illumination catches the scars across his face, turning them into pale lines against his ash-covered skin.

His gaze settles on your hand.

Then he looks at the glowing walls.

“Look what you did, little key,” he murmurs, his cold breath brushing the nape of your neck. “You just lit up this entire keep.”

You turn towards him. “I didn't mean to.”

“No. That's generally the problem with power that has been buried for generations.” His eyes narrow as another pulse of violet light travels through the floor. “You have been carrying a dormant key inside your blood, and now you've taught the lock to recognise it.”

The runes flare brighter.

A crack splits the granite beside the door. It is narrow at first, but light pours through it, revealing another layer of markings beneath the visible stone. These are different from the outer runes. Their lines are jagged and crowded, circling something that seems to have been deliberately concealed.

For one fleeting moment, you feel a presence beneath the keep.

Not a voice. Not a thought.

An awareness pressing against the other side of a sealed door.

Your knees threaten to buckle. The heat in your blood is no longer merely warmth; it is a current pulling at you, demanding that you follow the glowing channels towards their source.

Balor catches your wrist before you can reach for the wall.

“Don't touch anything else.”

His grip is cold, but the contact steadies you. The violet light gathers around your joined hands, and the runes nearest your feet brighten in response.

His expression changes.

For the first time since you met him, he looks genuinely uncertain.

“That should not have happened,” he says.

Above you, the high tower bell begins to toll.

The first strike shakes dust from the ceiling. The second is answered by the grinding of heavy gates throughout the keep. Metal shutters descend somewhere along the upper corridors. Boots pound across the stone, and a command rings out, sharp enough to carry through the entire structure.

“Seal the lower levels! Nobody enters or leaves without my order!”

Commander Vane.

You have seconds before the patrol breaches the cellar entrance by another route. The runes have exposed your presence to anyone who understands the old magic, and the keep is closing around you. Balor watches you with burning eyes, waiting to see whether you will trust him, flee him, or surrender yourself to the authorities.

Your hand still glows faintly in the violet light.

Whatever you have awakened, you cannot simply pretend it never happened.

How do you handle the sudden lockdown?

choices.text: Use the blinding violet flare to slip away into the dark lower tunnels alone.
Take the intruder's hand and use the activated foundation runes to break out through the outer wall.
Step back from the melted door and prepare to surrender to Commander Vane's guards.

text.content:
Commander Vane stands over the long oak map table in the High Keep, the flame of a tallow candle reflecting in his tired grey eyes. The garrison bell has finally ceased its toll, but the keep remains on high alert. Guards patrol the corridors in pairs, iron-shod boots striking against stone, while messengers hurry between the towers carrying reports of strange lights beneath the foundations.

The air smells of wax, wet wool, and cold iron.

You stand opposite Vane, your clothes still carrying the dust of the lower vaults. Your hands have stopped glowing, but the memory of that impossible heat remains beneath your skin. You keep them folded at your sides, careful not to reveal how much the experience has shaken you.

Vane studies you for a long moment.

“You proved your worth tonight,” he says at last. “Most people freeze when supernatural blood is spilled on stone. You raised the alarm, held your ground, and gave my men time to respond.”

He reaches into a leather case and removes a heavy brass badge. Its surface bears the emblem of Highspire Garrison: a tower enclosed within a ring of iron thorns. He slides it across the parchment map towards you.

“The mark of a Garrison Warden. You will answer directly to me until further notice.”

The badge feels heavier than it looks when you pick it up. It represents authority, but also obligation. The refugees in the lower courtyard are frightened and exhausted. The soldiers are stretched thin, and the Bone Coven's intentions remain unclear. Somewhere beyond the valley, an army may already be marching towards you.

“Why me?” you ask.

“Because you have seen what is happening beneath this keep, and because you haven't run screaming into the woods.” Vane taps the map with one thick finger. “I need people who can make decisions when everyone else is waiting for orders.”

His gaze sharpens.

“Do not mistake this appointment for trust. I don't know what the Coven wants with you, and I don't know why the old wards responded as they did. Until I understand both, you will remain under observation.”

You look down at the map. The valley is marked in faded ink, its roads and settlements connected by thin black lines. Highspire Garrison occupies the narrow northern pass, where steep hills funnel travellers towards the keep's outer gates. Small symbols indicate watchtowers, supply depots, and defensive positions. Beyond the pass, the forest spreads across the parchment in a wash of dark green, its deepest reaches left deliberately uncharted.

Vane follows your gaze.

“The Coven is moving towards this valley. Their scouts have been sighted along the eastern road, and my sentries report disturbances near the old boundary stones. Whatever was sealed beneath Highspire is no longer sleeping peacefully.”

He pauses, then lowers his voice.

“The scholars believe the old bindings are failing. If they collapse completely, we may be facing more than a Coven expedition. The creatures trapped beyond those wards were bound for a reason.”

You remember the presence you felt beneath the keep: something vast and aware, pressing against the other side of a sealed door. The thought makes your stomach tighten.

“Can the wards be repaired?” you ask.

“Perhaps. But the Coven has kept its methods secret for generations. They claim only their scholars understand the bindings. I suspect that is not the whole truth.”

His eyes settle briefly on your hands.

You realise he is watching for another flare of magic.

Before you can respond, a young officer enters the chamber carrying a stack of reports. He whispers something to Vane, who dismisses him with a curt nod. The commander's expression darkens as he reads the top page.

“Three wagons of cold iron are arriving before dawn,” he says. “We'll need every able hand to prepare the defences. The refugee quarter is overcrowded, the outer parapets are undermanned, and our dungeon prisoners may know more about the Coven's plans than they have admitted.”

He looks directly at you.

“You have authority over the lower gate watch. Use it wisely. We have one night to make this keep harder to break.”

The brass badge rests in your palm. For the first time since Highspire burned, you have a position, a purpose, and a chance to influence what happens next. Whether this is genuine security or simply a more comfortable form of captivity remains to be seen.

Vane rolls up his sleeves and leans over the map.

“Tell me how you intend to prepare our defences before dawn.”

choices.text: Fortify the refugee quarter first, ensuring civilians have armoured shelter.
Focus all resources on mounting cold-iron ballistas along the outer parapets.
Request permission to interrogate any Fae or Coven prisoners held in the dungeons.

text.content:
You learn quickly that Highspire Garrison has more weaknesses than its commanders would care to admit.

The first night, you walk the perimeter under the pretence of looking for spare blankets. The second, you carry a bucket towards the kitchens and take a longer route than necessary, counting the guards stationed along the inner wall. By the third night, you no longer need excuses. You have become another indistinct figure moving through the shadows, overlooked by soldiers too tired to question every passing refugee.

You memorise the rhythm of the garrison.

The western gate changes its watch just before midnight. Two guards patrol the southern wall, but one regularly disappears into the stairwell to warm his hands beside the kitchen ovens. The northern battlements are better defended, with crossbowmen stationed beneath iron lanterns, their weapons pointed towards the dark valley beyond.

The eastern wall is different.

It overlooks a steep river ravine, where black water rushes between jagged rocks far below. Few soldiers patrol that stretch because the terrain seems impassable. The wall itself is old, its foundations built from blocks of uneven granite that predate the garrison towers. Moss grows between the stones, and the wind carries the constant damp smell of the river.

You discover the drain grate on your fourth night.

It lies close to the base of the eastern wall, partially concealed behind a tangle of dead ivy. The iron bars are rusted, and one has pulled loose from the surrounding stone. Beneath it, a narrow drainage channel slopes towards the ravine. You cannot tell how far it extends, but the current of air rising through the opening suggests it connects to a larger network beneath the keep.

You test the loose bar with your fingers.

It shifts.

Not enough to open the grate, but enough to give you hope.

You begin assembling a private map in your head: the drain grate, the wall-walk above it, the blind corner beside the abandoned watchtower, the stairwell that leads down to the lower stores. You note where the lanterns leave gaps in the darkness and which guards seem most likely to notice a stranger.

You also learn what the garrison is preparing for.

Wagons arrive after sunset, their wheels wrapped in cloth to muffle the noise. Soldiers unload cold-iron stakes, sealed crates, and long metal cases that require two men to carry. Orders are issued in whispers. The armory doors remain locked, and anyone approaching the lower levels without permission is sent away under armed escort.

Whatever is happening beneath Highspire, the commanders expect trouble.

You have no intention of being caught in the middle of it.

The surviving villagers are safer inside the garrison than they would be wandering the countryside, but you have begun to doubt that safety will last. The Bone Coven has its secrets, Commander Vane has his orders, and the strange power stirring beneath the keep seems connected to your blood. If the authorities discover what you are, you may find yourself imprisoned rather than protected.

You decide that when the time comes to leave, you will not wait for permission.

On the fifth night, you climb the narrow steps to the eastern parapet shortly after midnight. The sky is clouded, hiding the moon, and the river below is little more than a faint roar in the darkness. You settle beside the old drain grate, keeping low beneath the broken crenellations.

From here, you can see most of the eastern approach. The nearest guard patrol passes at regular intervals, their lanterns sweeping across the stones. You count the seconds between their appearances and watch until their lights vanish around the northern tower.

Then you hear something.

A scrape of metal against stone.

You freeze.

The sound comes from beyond the wall, near the outer iron stakes driven into the earth along the ravine's edge. Those stakes are meant to deter intruders and disrupt supernatural crossings. Anyone attempting to pass them should trigger the warding charms attached to their bases.

No alarm sounds.

Instead, a dark shape rises above the parapet.

A hand grips the stone. A second follows. Then a figure vaults over the outer iron stakes and lands silently on the battlements, scarcely an arm's length away from you.

You press yourself against the cold granite, barely daring to breathe.

The intruder wears a dark cloak that blends into the night. Their movements are controlled and deliberate, suggesting someone who knows precisely where to place each foot. A faint glimmer catches along one sleeve before disappearing beneath the fabric.

They pause, head tilted, listening.

Then they turn towards the inner keep.

You cannot see their face, but you notice something unsettling: the iron stakes behind them have begun to glow faintly, their warding marks flickering as though they have been disturbed.

The intruder has crossed a boundary that should have been impossible to breach.

And they have done it without raising the alarm.

Your hand tightens around the small knife concealed in your belt. You could challenge them now, before they disappear into the keep. Alternatively, you could remain hidden and follow them, learning where they intend to go and who—or what—they have come to find.

The patrol will return soon. You have only moments to decide.

choices.text: Confront the shadow on the roof before it can slip into the keep.
Slip into the shadows and track the intruder from above.

text.content:
You see that the intruder is the same Fae you saw in Hishspire. Balor moves before you can decide whether to confront him or remain hidden.

You are too late to gain the advantage.

He turns with startling speed and catches your wrist before you can draw your weapon. His grip is cold and unyielding. You struggle instinctively, but he twists your arm just enough to stop you without breaking it.

For one breathless moment, you stand face-to-face beneath the clouded moon.

He smells of pine needles, damp earth, and cold night air. Ash streaks his cheek, and a dark hood conceals most of his features, though not the pale edge of an old scar along his jaw. His eyes, however, are unmistakable: a pale, unnatural glow that catches the faint light from the garrison lanterns.

Not human.

You have seen those eyes before, burning through the smoke of Highspire Square.

Your gaze flicks towards the iron stakes beyond the wall. Their warding marks still flicker faintly, but no alarm has sounded. Whatever Balor is, he has crossed the garrison's outer defences without triggering the protections.

Balor follows your glance, then looks down at your wrist.

“You have been busy.”

His voice is low, almost amused. He releases you, though he remains close enough to stop you reaching for your knife again.

You notice his attention shifting towards the drain grate. The loose iron bar has been moved slightly from where you left it. Beside it, the chalk marks you made to measure the gaps in the patrol's route are visible beneath the lantern light. A length of thin rope is tucked into a crack in the masonry, ready to be retrieved when you need it.

Balor studies these preparations with a faint, dangerous smile.

“You mapped the garrison's blind spot,” he says. “I came to break through their perimeter, but it looks like a mortal already built the back door.”

Your stomach tightens.

“You were watching me?”

“I was watching the walls.” His glowing eyes return to yours. “You simply happened to be doing something interesting.”

You consider shouting for the guards. The watch-horn at your belt would bring soldiers running within moments. But Balor has already demonstrated that ordinary defences mean little to him. You are not certain whether the guards would capture him—or merely give him an excuse to start killing.

Balor seems to read the calculation on your face.

“Before you decide to summon your friends, consider what happens next. They arrive with crossbows and cold iron. I defend myself. Someone falls over that wall, and Commander Vane spends the morning asking why his eastern watch has failed.”

“You broke through a warded perimeter,” you reply. “You expect me to let you wander around the keep?”

“No.” His smile fades. “I expect you to recognise that the people inside these walls are not necessarily the ones keeping you safe.”

The words strike closer than you would like.

You remember the locked armory, the secretive shipments of cold iron, and the strange heat that has been gathering beneath your skin since Highspire burned. You remember the way the garrison officers watch you when they think you are not looking. Whatever the Coven knows about your bloodline, it has not been shared freely.

Balor glances towards the central tower.

“Something beneath this keep is waking,” he says. “The wards are weakening, and the Coven is preparing to contain the consequences. They will tell your commander that everything they do is necessary. They may even believe it.”

“And you?” you ask. “What do you want?”

For the first time, Balor hesitates.

“To get through the perimeter without being surrounded by soldiers. To find what the Coven has hidden here. And to leave before the entire valley becomes a battlefield.”

“That tells me what you want. Not why I should trust you.”

“You shouldn't.”

The answer is immediate.

A gust of wind sweeps across the battlements, carrying the smell of wet stone and distant smoke. Somewhere below, a guard laughs at something his companion has said. The ordinary sound seems strangely fragile against the darkness gathering beyond the walls.

Balor steps back, giving you room to move.

“But you have an escape route,” he continues. “I know a way through the wards. You know the garrison's blind spots. We could help each other.”

His gaze settles on the drain grate once more.

“Or you can call your guards and discover whether Commander Vane considers you a loyal servant or a useful prisoner.”

Footsteps sound faintly from the northern stairwell. The next patrol is approaching.

You have only moments to choose whether Balor is a threat to be exposed or an opportunity too dangerous to ignore.

choices.text: Hold your ground on the moonlit parapet and trade your escape route for answers.
Blow the watch-horn at your belt to summon the parapet guards to the roof.

text.content:
You do not pull your hand away.

Balor's fingers are cold against yours, but the moment your skin touches his, a sudden, electric heat races up your arm. The dormant hum in your blood awakens, vibrating beneath your ribs. His glowing eyes widen slightly, and for a heartbeat neither of you moves.

He knows you felt it too.

Below the battlements, the river rushes through the ravine, black water foaming around jagged rocks. The wind pulls at your clothes, carrying the scent of pine from the forest beyond the garrison walls. Somewhere behind you, the approaching patrol clatters along the stone stairs.

“I mapped it so I could survive,” you whisper, glancing towards the drain grate. “Tell me what is coming for this garrison, and perhaps I'll let you use my door.”

The faint smile disappears from his face.

“Balor,” he says, offering the name as though it should mean something to you.

You stare at him. “I know who you are.”

“Then you know the Coven has been trying to put me back in a cage.”

He releases your hand, but he does not step away. In the dim light, you can see the silver-lit wounds beneath his torn clothing. His face is streaked with ash, and the scars crossing his cheek disappear beneath the edge of his hood. He looks exhausted, though there is nothing weak about the way he stands.

“What is coming,” he continues, “is the Bone Coven's siege engine. Not merely soldiers with ladders and iron-tipped arrows. They have brought machinery designed to strengthen the old bindings and force anything connected to them into submission.”

He looks towards the central keep.

“They know the key-blood is inside these walls. They know the wards have begun to answer it. And they will not allow that power to remain beyond their control.”

Your stomach tightens. “How do you know they are coming for me?”

“Because I heard them discussing it before I escaped their hunters.” His jaw hardens. “They intend to put you on these battlements when the siege begins. If the old wards respond to your blood, they will use you to draw out whatever remains beneath the keep. If you resist, they will find another way to make you useful.”

The cold wind seems to penetrate your clothes.

Commander Vane has given you a place within the garrison, perhaps even the beginnings of trust. Yet you cannot forget the secrecy surrounding the lower vaults or the way the soldiers watched you after the strange magic awakened beneath your skin.

“Why tell me this?” you ask. “What do you get out of helping me escape?”

Balor studies you for a moment.

“Your blood can open doors that have been sealed for centuries. Mine can survive the things waiting on the other side. Together, we might discover what the Coven has hidden.”

“That sounds remarkably convenient for you.”

A quiet laugh escapes him. It is brief, almost surprised, as though he had not expected you to challenge him.

“I did say you shouldn't trust me.”

He steps closer, drawing his heavy mantle around his shoulders. The movement shields you from the bitter wind, though whether he intends the gesture as protection or simply wants to keep the conversation private, you cannot tell. You become acutely aware of the small distance between you, the warmth of his body beneath the cold night air, and the strange pull that lingers wherever your hands nearly touch.

“Come with me now,” he says. “We descend into the ravine, follow the river until we reach the untamed wild, and disappear before the Coven seals the perimeter.”

You look down.

The drop is sheer, and the river below looks merciless. Even if you survived the fall, the current could drag you beneath the rocks before you found a place to climb out. Balor seems to read your expression.

“There is a ledge halfway down,” he says. “A narrow one. We can reach it from the broken section of wall, then lower ourselves to the water.”

“And if you're wrong?”

“Then we fall together.”

“You make that sound reassuring.”

“I have been told I am not particularly reassuring.”

Despite yourself, you almost smile.

The moment passes when a lantern appears at the far end of the parapet. The patrol is approaching, its light sweeping across the stone. Balor draws back into the shadows, but he does not retreat far enough to disappear.

“You have three choices,” he says quietly. “Stay here and let the garrison decide your fate. Use your hidden route to move through the keep and learn what the Coven is planning. Or come with me and discover the truth beyond these walls.”

His gaze drops briefly to your hand.

“Whatever you choose, the wards have already recognised you. There is no returning to the life you had before.”

The lantern light creeps closer. You can hear the guards talking now, their voices carrying over the wind. Balor extends his hand towards you, palm upward, leaving the decision entirely yours.

You could take it and abandon the garrison, trusting a dangerous stranger who has every reason to use your blood for his own purposes. You could refuse to leave, keeping your escape route secret while you gather information from within. Or you could test the ancient ward-stone beneath your feet and discover whether the power in your blood is truly what Balor claims.

The patrol turns the corner.

You have only moments to decide.

choices.text: Take his hand and jump into the river ravine together, fleeing the garrison tonight.
Refuse to jump tonight: use the secret drain route to act as a rogue courier inside the keep.
Touch the ancient ward-stone on the parapet to prove your bloodline's truth.

text.content:
The decision takes less than a heartbeat.

You wrench your wrist free and snatch the brass watch-horn from your belt. Balor’s glowing eyes narrow as you raise it to your lips, but he is a fraction too late. You blow.

The sound tears across the battlements, sharp and piercing, cutting through the gale like a blade. It echoes from the high keep’s towers and rolls down into the courtyard below. For one suspended moment, the entire garrison seems to hold its breath.

Then the alarms begin.

Torches flare along the wall-walk. Doors slam open. Boots hammer against stone as soldiers pour from the stairwells, crossbows raised and swords drawn.

“Intruder on the eastern rampart!” someone bellows.

Balor turns towards the first approaching guards. Moonlight catches the silver light gathering around his fingers, a radiance that makes the iron buckles on his clothes gleam like frost. A crossbow bolt whistles through the darkness.

He flicks a hand.

The bolt stops in midair, trembling inches from his face. For an instant, you see the force holding it there: fine silver threads stretched through the night, almost invisible against the moonlight. Then Balor twists his wrist, and the bolt spins backwards into the stone beside the soldier who fired it.

“Stay back!” you shout, though whether you mean the guards or Balor, you cannot quite tell.

Balor’s gaze snaps towards you.

His expression is no longer amused. The faint suggestion of a smile has vanished, replaced by something furious and wounded.

“You foolish, loyal little key.”

He seizes your collar and drags you towards him. Your boots skid on loose gravel, and suddenly the crumbling parapet is directly behind you. Beyond it, the ravine drops into darkness, the river below nothing more than a thin ribbon of reflected moonlight.

You grab his wrist. Beneath your fingers, his skin feels unnaturally cold, but the blood beneath yours surges with sudden heat. The familiar pressure at your collarbone flares, as if something inside you has recognised Balor and is straining against an invisible chain.

“They will string you up from these very battlements,” Balor hisses, “when they realise what your blood ignited.”

“I called the guards because you broke into the keep,” you manage. “What did you expect?”

“The truth to matter?”

His laugh is bitter enough to silence you.

Behind him, soldiers advance in a tight formation, crossbows trained on Balor’s chest. At their centre, Commander Vane emerges onto the wall-walk, his sword drawn and his face pale with anger. He takes in the shattered ward-marks, the suspended bolt now embedded in stone, and Balor’s grip on your collar.

“Release them!” Vane commands.

Balor looks past you towards the commander. Silver light spreads from his hands, crawling over the stones in branching veins. The ward-marks carved into the battlements flicker in answer, first white, then violet. The air fills with the smell of scorched metal.

“You should have left this place buried,” Balor says.

He thrusts his free hand against the parapet.

The blast hits like a thunderclap.

Stone explodes outwards. A section of the wall-walk collapses, throwing soldiers off their feet and sending broken blocks tumbling into the ravine. You are flung sideways. Your shoulder strikes the ground hard enough to steal your breath, and the watch-horn clatters from your hand.

For a moment, the world is nothing but ringing ears, flying grit, and the groan of ancient masonry giving way.

You scramble backwards, palms scraping over the stone. A guard lies sprawled near the stairwell, clutching his arm. Another hauls himself away from the broken edge while shouting for help. Balor stands amid the wreckage, silver light pouring from his hands and illuminating the cracks spreading beneath his boots.

His eyes meet yours one final time.

There is no triumph in them. Only warning.

Then he leaps.

His silhouette drops beyond the ruined parapet and vanishes into the darkness of the ravine. No cry follows. No impact reaches you from below. Only the river continues its distant rush, indifferent to the destruction above it.

You stagger to your feet as the remaining guards surround you. Crossbows point towards your chest. A soldier grips your arm, though he seems uncertain whether he is restraining a witness or a potential threat.

Commander Vane steps over a broken block of stone. His expression is controlled, but the fury in his eyes is unmistakable.

“You sounded the alarm,” he says.

“Yes.”

“And yet the intruder reached the eastern rampart, broke through our wards, and escaped after destroying part of my wall.”

The commander glances at the violet light fading from the cracks. For the briefest instant, something like fear crosses his face.

“What,” he asks quietly, “did you tell them about this keep?”

You could explain that Balor already knew the garrison’s weaknesses. You could tell him about the eastern drain, the failing wards, and the way Balor spoke as though your blood belonged to him. But you remember the warning: They will string you up when they realise what your blood ignited.

You do not know whether Balor was threatening you, trying to protect you, or simply telling the truth in the cruelest way possible.

Below, the garrison begins to stir in earnest. Bells ring from the inner tower. Orders pass from one officer to another, and the ruined parapet is sealed off with armed guards. Whatever happened here will not remain a private matter for long.

Vane holds out his hand.

“The notes you were making about the eastern defences,” he says. “Give them to me. All of them.”

Your stomach tightens.

You had marked the guard rotations, the loose bar in the drain grate, and the places where the ward-lines flickered. Those notes could help the garrison protect itself. They could also reveal how easily someone might slip inside—or out.

The commander waits.

You have only a few seconds to decide what he will learn.

choices.text: Claim credit for spotting the infiltrator to earn a promotion in the garrison hierarchy.
Use the structural damage to the parapet to hide your secret notes before Vane's men search you.

text.content:
The alarm bells howl across Highspire Garrison, their iron tongues hammering out a warning that seems to shake dust from the ancient stones. Orders echo through the corridors above. Boots thunder across the courtyard, and somewhere beyond the walls, a horn answers from the darkness.

You are already gone.

You slip through a narrow service door concealed behind a stack of broken crates, turning sideways to squeeze into the passage beyond. The door closes with a soft click. At once, the noise of the garrison dulls, muffled by layers of stone and timber until the bells become little more than a distant vibration beneath your feet.

The passage smells of damp earth, old mortar, and something faintly metallic. You carry no lantern. You have learned that light attracts attention, and attention is the one thing you cannot afford.

You move by memory, fingertips brushing the uneven wall.

Highspire Garrison was built over older foundations. The soldiers know the official corridors, the watchmen know their assigned patrols, and the quartermasters know every storeroom listed in their ledgers. But the narrow passages between those spaces belong to no map. They were built for servants to carry coal and water, for masons to reach hidden supports, and perhaps for someone to move unseen when the gates were barred.
You know them because you have spent nights watching the garrison rather than sleeping.
You know them because you have spent nights watching the garrison rather than sleeping.
You know them because you have spent days in the armory, learning which doors need keys and which corridors the guards ignore.
You know them because you have spent days in the armory, learning which doors need keys and which corridors the guards ignore.
At the first junction, you pause and listen.

Two guards pass on the other side of the wall, arguing about the collapsed parapet. One insists the intruder must have been a Fae scout. The other says no Fae could have crossed the outer wards without setting off every alarm in the keep.

Neither mentions the violet light.

Neither mentions the way the stones answered it.

Two guards pass on the other side of the wall, arguing about the breach in the eastern wards. One insists the intruder must have been a Fae scout. The other says no Fae could have crossed the outer stakes without setting off every alarm in the keep.

Neither mentions a second figure on the parapet.

Neither mentions the loose bar in the eastern drain.

Two guards pass on the other side of the wall, arguing about the melted lock on the cellar door. One insists the intruder in the vaults must have burned it through. The other says no Fae could have made the old stones glow like that.

Neither mentions the hand that touched the lock.

Neither mentions the way the runes answered it.

Two guards pass on the other side of the wall, arguing about the barred door to the lowest sub-vault. One insists the bolt was thrown from the inside. The other says that makes no sense, since the only man with a key is the quartermaster, and he is the one locked out.

Neither mentions the violet light in the lock-plate.

Neither mentions the way the stones answered it.

You wait until their footsteps fade, then continue down the left-hand passage.

You are not a soldier. You have no uniform, no rank, and no oath binding you to Commander Vane. You are not a prisoner of the Bone Coven, though their marks are scratched into the mortar near the outer walls. Nor are you a willing servant of the Fae, whose scouts may be watching from the forest.

For now, you belong to no faction.

That makes you vulnerable. It also makes you dangerous.

At the next junction, you find a narrow cupboard behind a loose panel. Inside are three folded blankets, a coil of twine, a flint striker, and a small sack of dried apples. The quartermaster hides emergency supplies here, away from the official stores. You take the flint and two apples, leaving the rest untouched. If anyone discovers the cupboard has been disturbed, you want them to believe it was rats.

Beyond the cupboard, a steep set of steps descends towards the foundations.

The air grows colder with every step. You feel the familiar pressure beneath your collarbone, a slow pulse that answers something deep below the keep. You stop with one hand against the wall.

There it is again.

Not a sound, exactly. More like a second heartbeat travelling through the stone.

You remember Balor on the parapet, silver light spilling from his hands. You remember the ward-marks flaring violet, and the terrible ease with which he shattered a wall that had stood for generations.
You remember Balor's cold fingers against yours on the parapet, and the way your blood answered before he had said a word. You remember the river rushing far below, and the hand he held out to you.

You remember the iron lock melting beneath your palm, and the violet runes racing through the stone like veins. You remember Balor catching your wrist, and the way he looked genuinely uncertain for the first time.
You remember the lock-plate pulsing beneath your skin like a key turning in your bones. You remember the iron door sliding shut, and Harlowe's face on the other side of it.

Whatever is buried beneath Highspire, the garrison's defences are connected to it. Perhaps the keep was built to protect the secret. Perhaps it was built to contain it.

Either possibility makes the coming dawn more dangerous.

At the foot of the steps, the passage divides. One branch leads towards the armory vaults, where cold iron is stored behind barred doors. Another slopes towards the eastern drain, a narrow channel running beneath the outer wall before emptying into the ravine. The third ends at a bricked-up doorway bearing a faint mark you recognise from the outer mortar: three intersecting lines scratched into a circle.

A Bone Coven boundary mark.

You crouch to inspect it. The mark has been cut recently. Fresh pale dust lies on the floor beneath it, and a thin line of grey wax seals a crack between two stones. Someone has been working here in secret.

You touch neither the wax nor the mark. Instead, you commit their position to memory.

The Coven is not merely preparing to defend the garrison. Its people are moving through the foundations, altering wards, and concealing their work from the soldiers who supposedly control the keep. Commander Vane may know more than he admits, but he clearly does not know everything.

You have three possible advantages: information, access, and the ability to move between factions without declaring yourself to any of them.

By dawn, one of those advantages could become a weapon. The question is whose hand will hold it.

A faint scraping sound travels through the drainage passage. You extinguish the flint's tiny glow beneath your cupped palm and wait. Somewhere beyond the eastern grate, a low whistle answers from the woods.

Three notes. A pause. Two more.

Not a bird.

You cannot tell whether the signal comes from a Fae scout, a Coven messenger, or someone else entirely. But whoever is outside knows this route exists.

You have little time to decide how to use what you know. The garrison is tightening its grip, the Coven is moving unseen beneath its feet, and the Fae are close enough to signal through the drains.

You can steal the commander’s maps, use the hidden route to make contact with the Fae, or intercept the Coven’s messenger before they reach the postern gate.

Each choice will make you useful to someone. None will leave you entirely free.

choices.text: Steal Commander Vane's tactical maps from the High Keep solar while guards are distracted.
Use the secret drainage route to smuggle supplies out to the Fae scouts in the woods.
Intercept the Bone Coven's secret messenger at the postern gate to buy your freedom.

text.content:
Marek’s Wardens clash with Balor’s starfire in the burning square, throwing long, violent shadows across the cobblestones. Iron strikes against silver light. The air fills with the shriek of tearing magic, the crack of splintering timber, and the desperate cries of villagers caught between two powers that seem to regard their lives as little more than an inconvenience.

You do not wait to see which side wins.

You turn and plunge into the dense, ash-choked canopy of the outer woods.

Branches whip across your face. Roots rise beneath your feet, threatening to send you sprawling, while smoke rolls between the trees in thick grey ribbons. Behind you, the village burns with an unnatural violet light, illuminating the forest in brief, feverish flashes. Every few seconds, the earth shudders beneath your boots as another building collapses or a spell strikes the square.

You have lived beside these woods for most of your life. You know the deer paths, the old boundary stones, the places where the ground turns marshy after rain. Yet tonight, familiar landmarks seem strangely misplaced. A crooked ash tree stands where you remember a cluster of hazel bushes. The stream you crossed as a child runs uphill for several yards before vanishing beneath a bank of blackened roots.

The forest is changing.

Or perhaps you are finally seeing what has always been there.

A dark shape moves ahead of you.

Balor.

His long coat cuts through the mist like a blade, its edges torn and scorched from the violence in the square. He moves with impossible speed, slipping between trees without disturbing the hanging branches. Every so often, silver light glimmers beneath the skin of his hands, illuminating the shattered rings around his wrists.

He does not look back to see whether you are keeping up.

To him, you are not a companion escaping a massacre. You are the key that stumbled out of its lock.

You grit your teeth and push harder.

A low branch catches your shoulder. You stumble, catch yourself against a tree, and glance over your shoulder. Through the gaps in the canopy, you can still see the violet glow above Highspire. The flames should be fading as the village burns down, but instead the light seems to grow brighter, pulsing in time with the heat beneath your collarbone.

Your blood answers it.

You press a hand against your chest, trying to steady the sudden rhythm. It feels as though something buried deep inside you has awakened and is straining towards the village, tugging at invisible threads connected to the burning square.

You force yourself to keep moving.

Balor finally stops beside a narrow ravine, where a stream tumbles over dark stones into a pool hidden beneath the roots of ancient trees. He turns sharply, and you nearly collide with him.

For the first time since you fled Highspire, he looks directly at you.

His eyes are unlike any mortal eyes you have ever seen. Their darkness is edged with a deep, banked silver, like stars reflected in the surface of a winter lake. Fine scars cross one cheek, disappearing beneath the collar of his coat. More mark his throat, where the skin appears almost translucent around faint lines of light.

The broken silver rings around his wrists are not ordinary jewellery. You can see that now. Each is inscribed with symbols too intricate to follow, and the metal seems to bite into his skin wherever it touches. One ring has split almost completely in two. The other remains intact, though a thin crack runs across its surface.

Balor catches you studying them.

“Admiring my restraints?” he asks.

His voice is quiet, but there is something dangerous beneath the words.

“You could have mentioned that we were running into the forest,” you reply, still catching your breath. “Or explained why an entire army wants to kill you.”

“Would either explanation have made you run faster?”

“That depends. Does the army want to kill you, or does it want to kill me?”

His expression changes slightly. It is not quite amusement, though something in his eyes suggests he appreciates the question.

“Both, eventually.”

The answer is delivered with such casual certainty that you almost laugh. You do not, because the sound of pursuit reaches you from somewhere behind the trees.

A horn sounds from the direction of Highspire. A second answers farther away, deeper in the forest. Then comes the unmistakable rhythm of boots on the old northern road.

The Wardens are spreading out.

Balor turns towards the sound, listening. Silver light flickers along the broken rings. For a heartbeat, you see something beneath his composure: pain, sharp and immediate. His hand closes around his wrist, and the light disappears.

“You are injured,” you say.

“I am inconvenienced.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“It is the distinction that matters.”

He starts walking again.

You follow, although every step takes you farther from the village and deeper into country you have never explored. The trees grow older here, their trunks broad enough to conceal a cottage. Pale lichen spreads across their bark in patterns that resemble written characters. Some of the roots rise from the ground in arches, creating dark hollows beneath them. The air smells of wet stone, crushed leaves, and something faintly sweet that reminds you of flowers left too long in a sealed room.

You pass a standing stone half swallowed by moss. Its surface is covered in shallow grooves. You recognise none of the markings, but the moment you draw level with it, the heat beneath your collarbone surges.

The stone answers with a faint violet glow.

Balor stops.

Slowly, he looks from the stone to you.

“What did you do?”

“Nothing.”

“Your blood disagrees.”

You step away from the stone. The light fades, leaving only moss and weathered rock.

Balor studies you for several seconds. Whatever he sees seems to confirm a suspicion he has carried for some time.

“Highspire was not the only lock,” he says at last. “And the village was not the only thing your blood could open.”

A chill passes through you that has nothing to do with the night air.

“What does that mean?”

“It means the Wardens will not stop hunting you merely because you have left their reach. Marek will send riders. He will send hounds trained to follow magic. If he believes you can open what lies beneath this forest, he may send something worse.”

“And you?”

“I have other uses for you.”

At least he does not pretend otherwise.

You look back towards the distant glow of Highspire. Somewhere in that burning village are the people you knew, the rooms you lived in, the ordinary objects that once made up your life. You do not know how many survived. You do not know whether Kael escaped the square, whether your family found shelter, or whether anyone will ever return to rebuild what was lost.

The uncertainty presses against your ribs more painfully than the cold.

Balor watches you without offering comfort. Perhaps he has none to give. Perhaps he simply sees grief as another obstacle to be crossed.

“You expect me to trust you,” you say.

“No.” He turns towards the deeper forest. “I expect you to survive long enough to decide whether I deserve it.”

For the first time, you notice that he has chosen a path that avoids the standing stones. He keeps to the darker ground between them, stepping carefully around exposed roots and patches of silver-grey moss. Whatever this place is, he knows its dangers.

You can follow him blindly and hope that his knowledge is enough to keep you alive. Or you can demand answers before allowing him to lead you any farther.

The sounds of pursuit grow louder behind you. Somewhere in the distance, a branch snaps. A moment later, another answers from the opposite side of the ravine.

The Wardens are closing in.

Balor glances back, his expression hardening.

“Choose quickly,” he says. “They are not coming here to offer you a place beside their hearth.”

You look at the silver rings biting into his wrists, at the ancient stones glowing faintly among the trees, and at the dark path that disappears beneath the canopy ahead.

You have escaped the burning village, but you have not escaped the forces that destroyed it. You are travelling beside a dangerous stranger who knows your blood is important, while the forest itself seems to recognise something in you that you do not understand.

The next decision may determine whether you remain your own person—or become the property of whichever power reaches you first.

choices.text: Confront his arrogance directly and demand answers about the silver rings on his wrist.
Focus entirely on silent survival, matching his breakneck pace through the dark.

text.content:
You stop dead on the damp moss, refusing to take another step until he acknowledges you.

Balor takes three more strides before realising you are no longer behind him. He halts, turning on his heel with a lethal, feline grace. The faint light beneath his skin catches his eyes, turning them red-gold in the darkness.

“What now?” he demands.

“What now?” you repeat, incredulous. “You drag me out of a burning village, tell me that armies want to kill me, refuse to explain what I am, and expect me to follow you into the woods like a faithful hound. I would like some answers.”

His expression hardens. “And I would like a night without Wardens, broken bindings, and mortals who mistake a dangerous situation for an appropriate moment to argue.”

“Then perhaps you should have chosen a different mortal.”

For a moment, neither of you moves.

The forest seems to draw closer around you. Water trickles somewhere below the ravine, and the wind stirs the branches overhead. The standing stones behind Balor give off the faintest violet shimmer, almost imperceptible beneath the moonlight. You can feel that strange pressure beneath your collarbone again, a steady pull towards something deeper in the woods.

Balor's gaze drops briefly to your chest.

“You can feel them, can't you?” he asks.

“Feel what?”

“The old bindings. The ones beneath the earth.” He steps closer, studying you with an intensity that makes you instinctively straighten. “You think you are demanding answers from me. You should be asking yourself why the stones recognise your blood.”

Before you can respond, the crunch of iron-shod boots echoes through the thicket.

Balor's head snaps towards the ridge.

The sound comes again, followed by the muted clatter of armour and the scrape of metal against stone. Voices drift between the trees. One man gives an order; another answers that the trail leads towards the ravine.

Marek's patrol is sweeping the ridge.

Balor's entire manner changes. The irritation vanishes, replaced by an alert stillness that makes him seem less like a man and more like a predator listening for prey. He catches your arm.

“Not another word.”

You wrench against his grip. “You don't get to—”

He lunges before you can finish.

His hand clamps firmly over your mouth, and he pulls you backwards against an ancient monolith. Your shoulder strikes the cold stone. Before you can twist away, he pins you there, his body shielding yours from the ridge while his other hand braces against the rock beside your head.

His palm is cold against your lips, like river stone in winter. Beneath the sharp scent of damp leather, you catch crushed pine and something metallic, like the air after lightning.

You glare up at him.

His face is close enough that you can see the fine silver lines beneath his skin, pulsing faintly around the scars on his throat. His jaw is clenched, and his eyes remain fixed on the trees beyond your shoulder. He does not look pleased to be holding you still. He looks as though he is calculating how many people he could kill before the others reached you.

The first Warden appears between the trees.

You stop struggling.

Three figures move along the ridge, their dark armour catching the moonlight in dull flashes. Each carries a long iron staff etched with pale symbols. The marks glow whenever they pass close to one of the standing stones, and the stones answer with a faint tremor that travels through the ground.

A fourth Warden follows, leading a lean, dark hound on a chain. Its nose stays close to the earth, and its ears twitch at every movement in the undergrowth.

“Here,” one of the Wardens says. “The trail turns east.”

“The creature was wounded,” another replies. “It cannot have gone far.”

“And the key?”

A pause follows.

“Marek wants the mortal alive. If the blood has awakened, we are not to risk damaging it.”

Your stomach tightens beneath Balor's hand.

The Warden's words settle over you with dreadful clarity. They are not searching for you because you witnessed the destruction of Highspire. They are searching for you because they believe something inside you belongs to them.

The hound stops.

Its head rises, and its nostrils flare.

Balor's hand presses more firmly against your mouth. His body remains motionless, but you feel a sudden tension in his arm. A faint silver light gathers beneath his wrist, illuminating the cracked ring there.

The hound takes a step towards the monolith.

You hold your breath.

A pulse of heat rises beneath your collarbone. The stone at your back answers with a low vibration, so deep that you feel it in your teeth. For one terrifying instant, you are certain the hound will hear it.

Then the animal whines and recoils.

The handler curses, hauling it away from the monolith. The hound resists, claws scraping over the earth, but it finally turns towards the ridge. The patrol continues past you, close enough that you can hear the leather creak at their shoulders and the faint clink of the iron charms hanging from their belts.

One Warden stops.

You can see his shadow stretched across the moss. His boots stand barely an arm's length away.

“Did you hear that?”

“Wind,” another answers.

“No. Something else.”

Balor lowers his head until his lips are almost against your ear.

“Breathe,” he whispers, so quietly that the word is scarcely more than air.

You realise you have been holding your breath for too long. You let it out slowly through your nose, forcing your body to remain still even as your heart hammers against your ribs.

The Warden waits another moment.

Then the patrol moves on.

The crunch of boots fades into the trees. The hound gives one final, unhappy whine before the sound disappears beyond the ridge. Even after the forest falls silent, Balor does not release you immediately. He watches the darkness, listening for any sign that the patrol might return.

You become painfully aware of the closeness between you: the pressure of his shoulder against yours, the warmth of his breath near your ear, the rigid tension in his body. Beneath your hand, the stone remains cold. Beneath his, your mouth is still covered.

At last, he looks down at you.

“Now,” he murmurs, “you may ask your questions.”

His hand remains in place for another heartbeat.

You have two choices. You can make it clear that his protection does not give him authority over you, or you can remain still long enough to discover what lies beneath his guarded composure.

choices.text: Glare up at him and break his grip the second the footsteps fade.
Match his stillness in the dark, letting your hand rest briefly against his chest.

text.content:
You do not waste breath on arguments. You match Balor’s breakneck speed step for step, slipping through tangled fern and low-hanging branches like a shadow.

The forest closes around you as you descend from the ridge. Brambles catch at your sleeves, and wet leaves brush your face, but you learn quickly to anticipate his movements. When he ducks beneath a fallen trunk, you follow. When he leaps across a narrow stream, you land on the same flat stones without breaking stride. You keep your breathing measured and your eyes on the ground ahead, refusing to let exhaustion make you careless.

Balor does not slow down for you.

Perhaps he expects you to stumble. Perhaps he assumes that a mortal who has spent a lifetime among cottages and fields will soon discover the limits of their endurance. Either way, you have no intention of giving him the satisfaction.

Behind you, a horn sounds from the ridge.

Another answers farther away.

The Wardens are spreading through the woods.

Balor changes direction abruptly, cutting between two ancient oaks and following a path so narrow that the branches almost meet overhead. You follow without hesitation. The ground beneath your feet becomes softer, the soil dark and spongy with centuries of fallen leaves. Here, the trees grow in strange formations, their trunks twisting away from patches of pale moss that shimmer faintly in the moonlight.

You have never seen this part of the forest.

Yet something about it feels familiar.

Not in the way of a path you have walked before, but in the way of a half-remembered dream. You recognise the curve of a root before you see it. You know where the ground will slope and where the next patch of brambles will catch your clothes. Once, when Balor veers towards a shallow depression hidden beneath ferns, you instinctively take the higher ground instead.

He notices.

His next glance back carries a flicker of genuine surprise.

“You have been here before?” he asks.

“No.”

“Then how did you know to avoid that hollow?”

You look towards the depression. Nothing moves among the ferns, but a thin grey mist hangs above the earth. It curls inwards rather than drifting with the wind, disappearing through a narrow crack between two exposed roots.

“I don't know,” you admit.

Balor studies you for a moment, then looks away.

“Of course you don't.”

His tone irritates you, but you keep moving. There will be time to demand explanations when you are no longer being hunted.

The forest grows quieter as you travel deeper. The distant shouts of the Wardens fade, followed by the clatter of their armour. Soon, the only sounds are your footsteps, the whisper of branches, and the occasional rush of water beneath the ground.

Then the air changes.

You notice it first on your tongue: a cold, metallic taste, like blood touched by iron. The warmth beneath your collarbone begins to pulse, slow at first, then with increasing insistence. Each beat seems to answer something ahead of you, drawing you deeper into the trees.

Balor stops beside a standing stone.

Unlike the weathered markers near Highspire, this one is tall and narrow, its surface almost entirely covered in silver-carved symbols. The markings run from its pointed crown to the moss-covered base, forming patterns that seem to shift whenever you look directly at them. The stone stands at the edge of a shallow ridge, beyond which the forest descends into a valley filled with pale mist.

Balor places his hand against the stone.

The silver rings around his wrists flicker.

For a moment, the light beneath his skin brightens, and you see the strain it costs him. His fingers tremble against the carved surface before he withdraws them. One of the broken rings has cut into his wrist, leaving a thin line of luminous blood.

“You should keep moving,” he says.

“You sound as though you are afraid of this place.”

His eyes narrow.

“I am afraid of many things. I simply prefer not to advertise them.”

It is the closest thing to honesty he has offered you.

You look beyond the standing stone. On the opposite side of the valley, a high crag rises above the trees. Its dark face is broken by pale arches and narrow towers, their outlines visible against the moon. At first, you mistake them for natural rock formations. Then you notice the symmetry: columns carved into the cliff, balconies suspended above empty air, and a great circular arch crowned with silver shapes like intertwined branches.

Ruins.

Not mortal ruins. No village mason could have shaped stone so delicately, nor built structures that seem to grow from the cliff itself. Even from this distance, the architecture possesses an unsettling grace, as though the buildings were designed for creatures who moved through the air as easily as you walk upon the ground.

Balor follows your gaze.

Something guarded passes across his face.

“Those are older than your kingdom,” he says. “Older than the Coven. Older than the wars that taught your people to fear what they cannot control.”

“Fae ruins?”

He does not answer immediately.

The silence is answer enough.

You look back at the silver rings around his wrists. “And they bound you?”

“They bound many of us.”

His voice has lost its earlier sharpness. Beneath it lies something colder than anger: a grief so old that it has become part of him.

Before you can ask more, a low vibration travels through the earth. It begins as a faint tremor beneath your boots, then deepens into a steady hum that seems to rise through your bones. The standing stone vibrates in response. Silver symbols flare along its surface, and the warmth beneath your collarbone surges so sharply that you gasp.

Balor turns towards you.

“What did you touch?”

“Nothing.”

“Your blood is answering something.”

The hum grows stronger.

Below the ridge, the mist in the valley begins to move. It gathers into long, pale ribbons that coil around the roots of the trees. For an instant, you see thin lines of violet light threading through the ground, converging somewhere beneath the ravine. They resemble veins beneath translucent skin, pulsing with a rhythm that matches your heartbeat.

You understand, suddenly, that the forest is not merely hiding old ruins. Something runs beneath it, something vast and ancient that the stones were built to contain—or perhaps to guide.

Balor watches the light with an expression you cannot decipher.

“We have crossed the boundary,” he says. “The deep wild does not belong to the Coven, and their iron wards cannot reach everywhere. But the old places have their own rules.”

“And what happens if I break them?”

His gaze settles on you.

“Then we discover why your blood was hidden for so long.”

The hum divides into two distinct directions. One rises towards the crag, where the silver-carved ruins wait above the trees. The other descends into the misty ravine, where the violet lines pulse beneath the earth.

Balor waits for your decision. For the first time since you fled Highspire, he does not choose the path for you.

You can investigate the remnants of the Fae civilisation that once ruled this land, or follow the raw magic drawing you beneath the forest. Either route may bring you closer to the truth, but neither promises that you will remain unchanged.

choices.text: Steer him toward the ancient, silver-carved Fae ruins visible on the high crag.
Follow the deep, vibrating hum of raw leyline magic down into the misty ravine.

text.content:
The temple emerges from the mist like the skeleton of something too ancient to die.

You reach it shortly before midnight, following a narrow path that winds between twisted trees and slabs of pale stone. The structure stands in a hollow beneath the high crag, its roof long since collapsed and its outer walls swallowed by ivy. Silver carvings cover the remaining pillars, catching the moonlight in thin, cold lines. Beyond the broken entrance, the darkness seems unusually deep, as though the shadows have gathered here and chosen not to leave.

Balor pauses at the threshold.

For the first time since you fled Highspire, he appears reluctant to enter.

You glance at him. “I thought you knew these woods.”

“I do.”

“And this place?”

His jaw tightens. “I know enough.”

It is not an answer, but you have begun to suspect that most of his answers are carefully measured portions of a much larger truth.

You step inside.

The air changes immediately. The metallic taste that has followed you through the forest sharpens, mingling with the scent of wet stone and something faintly sweet, like flowers pressed between the pages of an old book. Your boots disturb a thin layer of silver-grey dust. Broken tiles lie scattered across the floor, their surfaces marked with the same intricate patterns carved into the standing stones outside.

The temple must once have been magnificent. Pillars rise along either side of the central hall, each carved with twisting branches, crescent shapes, and mirrored figures whose faces have been worn smooth by time. At the far end stands an altar of pale stone, split down the middle by a jagged crack. Behind it, the remains of a circular arch frame the misty forest beyond.

There are no statues of gods. No offerings. No signs of worship that you recognise.

Instead, every carving seems to turn towards the altar.

You look back at Balor.

He has remained near the entrance, arms crossed, his expression carefully blank. The broken silver rings around his wrists catch the moonlight, their etched symbols almost identical to those covering the pillars. He stares into the mist beyond the doorway as though the temple holds nothing worth examining.

Yet his fingers have curled tightly against his sleeves.

“You can come inside,” you say. “The stones won't bite.”

“An observation based on extensive experience?”

“An observation based on the fact that you are standing in the doorway looking as though you'd rather face Marek's entire patrol.”

That earns you a brief, humourless smile.

“I have faced worse than Marek.”

“I'm sure you have.”

You move farther into the hall, studying the carvings. Their precision fascinates you. Every line is repeated on the opposite side of the pillar, reflected so perfectly that the pattern appears to continue into itself. In places, the silver inlay has darkened. In others, it remains bright, untouched by centuries of weather.

You recognise the symbols around Balor's wrists among them.

The sight sends a small, uneasy thrill through you. The rings were not simply restraints made by the Bone Coven. Their design belongs to something older, something that existed before the village, before the garrison, perhaps before the kingdoms that now claim these woods.

“Balor.”

He does not turn.

“What are these markings?”

“Old script.”

“Can you read it?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

“And I am not going to translate every inscription you find interesting.”

You give him a flat look. “You are remarkably good at making yourself difficult to help.”

“I have survived this long without your help.”

“Have you? Because from where I'm standing, you look as though your own wrists are slowly cutting you apart.”

His gaze snaps to yours.

For a moment, the air between you tightens. You have touched something he did not intend to expose, and the silence that follows is more revealing than any answer could have been.

Then he looks away.

“Leave the altar alone,” he says.

Naturally, you look at it.

The central stone is smooth except for the deep crack running through its middle. Mirrored carvings spiral outwards from a small depression at its centre, their lines converging around a symbol you recognise from the silver rings. The pattern resembles two interlocking circles, one whole and one broken.

You approach slowly.

The closer you get, the warmer your skin becomes. The pressure beneath your collarbone returns, gathering into a steady pulse that seems to answer the altar's silent presence. You raise your hand, intending only to trace the edge of the carving.

Your fingertips touch the stone.

White light erupts through the temple.

The pillars flare simultaneously, their silver lines blazing so brightly that the entire hall becomes a field of reflected brilliance. The floor vibrates beneath your feet. Somewhere above, loose stones tumble from the broken arch, striking the ground with sharp cracks.

You jerk backwards, but before you can pull away, Balor crosses the hall in a fraction of a second.

His hand closes around your wrist.

The grip is crushingly firm, his fingers locking just above your pulse as he tears your hand away from the altar. The light vanishes almost as quickly as it appeared, leaving the temple in darkness except for the moonlight filtering through the broken roof.

You stumble against him.

His other hand catches your waist before you can fall. For one suspended moment, you are pressed against his chest, your wrist trapped in his grasp and your free hand braced against the front of his coat.

He is breathing hard.

So are you.

His face is close enough for you to see the fine lines of exhaustion around his eyes, the silver scars disappearing beneath his collar, and the faint glow that still moves beneath his skin. His expression is no longer detached. Fear, anger, and something far more difficult to name have broken through his composure.

“Are you trying to get yourself killed?” he demands.

“You told me to leave it alone. You didn't say touching it would set the entire temple on fire.”

“It didn't set the temple on fire.”

“An important distinction.”

His eyes narrow, but his hand remains around your wrist.

You feel his thumb resting against your pulse point. Beneath his touch, your heartbeat seems impossibly loud. The warmth under your collarbone has spread through your chest, and you become acutely aware of the closeness between you: the solid line of his body, the warmth of his breath against your cheek, the tension in his arm as he holds you steady.

He looks down at where your skin meets his.

Something flickers across his face.

His grip loosens, though he does not release you immediately.

“You should not be able to wake this place,” he says quietly.

“Why?”

“Because it was built to recognise those who made the bindings. Not those trapped inside them.”

His words settle between you.

You glance at the altar. The mirrored carvings have gone dark, but a single silver line remains illuminated in the central crack. It pulses once, in time with your heartbeat.

Balor follows your gaze. His expression closes again, the brief vulnerability disappearing behind familiar coldness. Yet his fingers linger at your wrist for one moment longer before he finally lets go.

You could ask about the ritual that bound him here, forcing him to confront the history he is so determined to conceal. Or you could challenge the distance he has rebuilt between you, making him admit that your touch affected him as much as the altar did.

choices.text: Ask him directly about the ritual that bound him: "Is this where they put the rings on you?"
Challenge his distance: "You flinched, Courtier. Does my touch rattle you so much?"

text.content:
Night settles over the wild without ever becoming entirely dark.

The trees stand in close ranks around your camp, their branches interlocking overhead until the moon appears only in fragments between the leaves. Mist drifts through the hollows, silver at its edges, and the distant sounds of the forest seem strangely muted. Even the stream below the shrine has fallen quiet, its earlier rush reduced to a soft murmur beneath the roots.

You sit beside a small, smokeless fire that burns with a pale amber glow.

Balor refuses to sit.

He paces the perimeter of the camp with the restless precision of a caged animal, checking the dark between the trees, pausing to listen, then moving again. The broken silver rings at his wrists catch the firelight whenever he turns. Occasionally, his fingers close around one of them, and a faint line of light travels beneath his skin before vanishing into his sleeve.

You have stopped asking him whether he is tired.

The first time you did, he looked at you as though you had asked whether stone becomes weary of being a mountain. Fae of his standing, he explained, have little use for mortal sleep.

You suspect that was not the whole truth.

There are many things Balor tells you with absolute confidence. There are just as many he avoids telling you at all.

You pull your cloak more tightly around your shoulders and stare into the flames.

He caught me before I fell.

The thought arrives uninvited.

You immediately try to dismiss it. Anyone standing close enough would have caught you. You had been about to stumble, the temple had been shaking, and Balor had reacted quickly. There is nothing remarkable about that.

Except that he crossed the entire hall before you had time to draw breath.

Except that his hand remained at your waist after you had regained your balance.

Except that, for one brief moment, he had looked at you as though the possibility of your being hurt was something he could not tolerate.

You shift uncomfortably.

He needs me alive.

That explanation is considerably more sensible. He has called you a key more than once. Whatever lies beneath the forest, whatever the ancient bindings conceal, your blood appears to matter to him. Perhaps he fears losing the only means he has of achieving whatever he has planned.

You glance at his wrists.

The rings are not decorative. Their edges have broken his skin, and the silver light beneath the metal seems to pulse with a rhythm of its own. You remember the way the altar answered your touch, and the sudden change in his expression when he realised what had happened.

He knows more about you than he is willing to admit.

But does he know what he intends to do with you?

That question troubles you more than the others.

Balor pauses at the edge of the clearing. His head turns slightly, and you have the uncomfortable impression that he has heard every thought passing through your mind.

Ridiculous. You cannot possibly know that.

Then his gaze settles on you.

You look down at the fire a moment too late.

Wonderful, Elara. You've survived a village burning, escaped an armed patrol, and discovered that your blood can wake ancient magic. Now you're embarrassed because a dangerous Fae man caught you looking at him.

You press your lips together.

There is something deeply unfair about his appearance. Even exhausted, even with blood drying beneath the broken rings, he carries himself with a composure that makes the surrounding forest seem less certain of its own existence. His dark coat is torn at one shoulder. His hair falls untidily across his forehead, and a narrow scar cuts through one eyebrow. He looks less like the terrifying figure who emerged from violet fire and more like someone who has spent too long surviving things he should never have had to endure.

You remind yourself that appearances are not evidence of character.

You remind yourself that he threatened you in the village square.

You remind yourself that he has repeatedly referred to you as a key.

All of these things remain true.

Unfortunately, so does the memory of his hand around your wrist, the startling warmth of his body against yours, and the way his voice had changed when he asked whether you were trying to get yourself killed.

You look back at the fire.

This is not attraction. It is adrenaline. Exhaustion. The natural response to being thrown into a dangerous situation with someone who might be the difference between life and death.

The explanation sounds convincing.

It also sounds suspiciously like something you are telling yourself because the alternative is inconvenient.

A twig snaps beyond the clearing.

Balor moves instantly. One moment he is standing beside a tree; the next, he is between you and the sound, one hand raised as silver light gathers along his fingers.

You stop breathing.

Nothing emerges from the darkness.

After several seconds, a small animal scurries through the undergrowth and disappears between the roots. Balor watches until it is gone, then lowers his hand.

“You can relax,” he says without looking at you.

“I was relaxed.”

He turns his head.

“You were gripping that stick as though you intended to challenge the entire forest with it.”

You look down. A half-burned branch lies clenched in your fist.

You place it beside the fire with as much dignity as possible.

“I prefer to be prepared.”

“So I have noticed.”

There is a trace of amusement in his voice. It catches you off guard, and you nearly smile before remembering that you are not supposed to find him amusing.

He notices that, too.

His expression changes—not into a smile, exactly, but into something quieter. For a few seconds, he simply watches you.

You expect him to make another remark. Instead, he returns to his slow circuit of the clearing.

That is somehow worse.

You find yourself wondering what he sees when he looks at you. Does he see the bloodline that can awaken ancient shrines? The mortal who might help him escape his bindings? Or does he occasionally forget, as you sometimes forget, that your meeting began with fire and violence?

Perhaps the question is meaningless. Balor has lived through centuries, if the old stories are even remotely true. You are a woman from a village that no longer exists. Whatever he feels, if he feels anything at all, it cannot carry the same weight for him that it might for you.

And yet he keeps looking back.

Once, when you raise your eyes, he is already watching you through the thin veil of heat rising from the fire. He does not look away when you meet his gaze. His expression is unreadable, but there is no mockery in it, no impatient calculation.

Only a quiet, complicated intensity that makes your chest tighten.

You hold his gaze for a moment longer than is comfortable.

Then you wonder whether he is testing you, measuring your willingness to challenge him, or simply waiting for you to make the first mistake.

Do not mistake attention for affection, you tell yourself. And do not mistake a moment of tenderness for trust.

The words settle you, though they do not entirely silence the questions.

The fire gives a soft crackle. Far away, something answers with a low, resonant hum. You feel it beneath your feet before you hear it properly, a vibration travelling through the ground from somewhere deep within the forest.

Balor's expression hardens.

He turns towards the sound, and the silver rings around his wrists begin to glow.

“What is that?” you ask.

“The leyline.”

You wait for him to explain.

He looks at you over his shoulder. “You will need to learn to recognise it. Your blood has already begun answering.”

“And you intend to teach me?”

“I intend to keep you alive.”

“That wasn't what I asked.”

“No,” he says quietly. “It wasn't.”

For a moment, neither of you speaks.
